analogy.p: Imagine a sorting belt at a recycling centre: everything small falls through a mesh onto a second belt (filtration), then workers pick the valuable items back off the belt and return them (selective reabsorption), while rubbish and the surplus water carries on to the bin (urine). A manager (ADH) tells the workers how much water to take back depending on how dry the factory is. The analogy breaks down because the kidney's pickers use energy-driven active transport and the manager is a hormone in the blood rather than a person giving orders.
analogy.t: A recycling centre with a conveyor belt

bullets: Waste products of metabolism must be removed because they are **toxic** or change the balance of the body.
**Carbon dioxide** from respiration is removed in exhaled air by the **lungs**.
**Urea** (from the breakdown of excess amino acids) is removed by the **kidneys** in urine.
**Water and ions** are lost in sweat, breath (water), and urine; the kidneys control how much is lost in urine.
**Excretion** (removal of metabolic waste) is different from **egestion** (removal of undigested food, faeces).
This content is **Biology triple (separate science) only**.
Linked idea: homeostasis; kidneys keep **water, ion and urea concentrations** of the blood within limits.
core.h: Excretion and waste products: what must be removed
core.p: **Excretion** is the removal of waste products of metabolism from the body. Cells constantly make waste substances that are harmful if they build up, so the body has organs that remove them. The two main waste products you must know are **carbon dioxide**, made in respiration and removed by the **lungs**, and **urea**, made in the liver and removed by the **kidneys** in **urine**. The body must also balance the amount of **water** and **mineral ions** (such as sodium ions): water and ions are taken in by food and drink and lost in several ways, and the kidneys adjust how much is lost in the urine so that the total in the body stays constant (homeostasis).

bullets: Water is lost via **lungs (breath)**, **skin (sweat)** and **urine** (plus a little in faeces).
Ions such as **sodium ions** are lost in **sweat** and **urine**.
Hot weather and exercise → more sweat → less urine, more concentrated.
Drinking a lot → more urine, more dilute (pale).
Water is gained from **drink, food** and a little from **respiration**.
**Water balance**: water in = water out on average; the kidneys provide the fine control.
If the water or ion content of the body is wrong, **too much water may move into or out of cells by osmosis**, damaging them.
core.h: Water leaves the body in several ways
core.p: Water is lost from the body through the **lungs** (as water vapour in exhaled air), through the **skin** (as **sweat**) and in **urine** produced by the kidneys. A small amount is also lost in faeces. The amount lost in sweat depends on temperature and exercise, and the amount lost in breath rises when breathing is faster. Because the body cannot control sweat and breathing losses to maintain water balance, the **kidney** adjusts the volume and concentration of urine to compensate. When more water is lost in sweat, less urine is produced and it is **more concentrated**; when a lot of water is drunk, **more urine** is produced and it is **more dilute**.

bullets: Excess amino acids cannot be stored; they are broken down in the **liver**.
**Deamination** = removal of the amino group from the amino acid, forming **ammonia**.
**Ammonia is toxic** and is immediately turned into **urea** (less toxic).
Urea is carried by the **blood plasma** to the kidneys.
The kidneys remove urea from the blood and it leaves the body in **urine**.
The liver also breaks down other substances, but only **urea formation** is needed at GCSE.
Higher protein intake increases the amount of urea produced.
core.h: Deamination: how urea is made in the liver
core.p: Amino acids from the digestion of protein are used to build new proteins, but the body cannot **store** excess amino acids. Excess amino acids are broken down in the **liver** in a process called **deamination**, in which the **amino group** is removed. This forms **ammonia**, which is **toxic**, so the liver immediately converts the ammonia into **urea**, which is much less harmful. The urea is released into the **blood plasma** and carried to the **kidneys**, which filter it out of the blood and excrete it in the urine.

bullets: Kidneys **filter the blood** and then **reabsorb** the useful substances.
They produce **urine**, which contains urea, excess ions and water.
Urine passes down the **ureter** to the **bladder** where it is stored, then out through the **urethra**.
Blood enters via the **renal artery** and leaves via the **renal vein** (with less urea).
The main roles are **removal of urea** and **regulation of water and ion content**.
A very large volume of blood passes through the kidneys every day.
core.p: The kidneys filter the blood and produce urine. Blood flows into each kidney in the **renal artery**, passes through many tiny filtering units, and leaves in the **renal vein**. The process has two main stages: **filtration**, in which small molecules are forced out of the blood, and **selective reabsorption**, in which the useful substances are taken back into the blood. What is left behind, with excess water, passes to the **bladder** as **urine**, which is stored and then released through the urethra. The kidneys therefore regulate the concentration of water, ions and urea in the blood.

bullets: Filtration is based on **molecule size**, not on whether the substance is useful.
Passing into the tubule: **water, urea, ions, glucose**.
Staying in the blood: **proteins, blood cells (red cells, white cells, platelets)**.
The blood is under **high pressure** which forces small molecules out.
The filtrate is **not yet urine** because it contains substances the body needs.
If protein or blood appears in urine this may show that the **filter is damaged**.
core.p: In the first stage, blood is forced under **high pressure** through tiny filters in the kidney. **Small molecules**, including **water, urea, glucose and ions**, pass out of the blood into the kidney tubule. **Larger molecules** such as **proteins** and **blood cells** are too big to pass through, so they stay in the blood. At this stage the filtrate contains useful substances (like glucose) as well as waste, because the filter works by **size**, not by usefulness. The kidney then has to reclaim the useful ones in the next stage.

bullets: **All glucose** is reabsorbed (by active transport).
**Some ions** are reabsorbed; the **excess** stays in the tubule and leaves in urine.
**Water** is reabsorbed to the amount the body needs (controlled by ADH).
**Urea is not reabsorbed** (mostly), so it stays in the tubule and leaves in urine.
Active transport = movement **against** a concentration gradient using **energy from respiration**.
Cells in the kidney tubule have many **mitochondria** to supply energy for this.
If glucose appears in urine it suggests the person may have **diabetes** (the kidney cannot reabsorb it all).
core.p: After filtration the kidney tubule takes back (**reabsorbs**) the substances the body needs. **All of the glucose** is reabsorbed into the blood, so none normally appears in urine. **Some of the ions** are reabsorbed (the amount depends on what the body needs), and **as much water as the body needs** is reabsorbed. Glucose and some ions are moved back into the blood by **active transport**, which needs energy from respiration, because they are moved against their concentration gradient. Because reabsorption is selective, the final urine is **different from the filtrate**.

bullets: Urine = **urea + excess ions + excess water**.
Normally contains **no glucose** and **no protein**.
Varies in **volume and concentration** to keep the blood's water content stable.
Dehydrated → **concentrated** urine, darker colour, small volume.
Over-hydrated → **dilute** urine, pale colour, larger volume.
The kidneys can change the concentration of ions in the blood by changing how much is excreted.
core.h: Urine: what it contains and how it varies
core.p: The liquid that leaves the kidneys, **urine**, is made of the substances that were **not** reabsorbed: **urea, excess ions and excess water**. The volume and concentration of urine vary according to how much water the body needs to keep. After sweating or not drinking, urine is **dark, small in volume and concentrated**. After drinking a lot, urine is **pale, large in volume and dilute**. Urine is normally free of glucose and protein, so testing urine can give clues about disease.

bullets: ADH is made/released by the **pituitary gland** in response to the **brain** detecting the blood water content.
ADH makes the **kidney tubules more permeable to water**.
More ADH → **more water reabsorbed** → **less, concentrated urine**.
Less ADH → **less water reabsorbed** → **more, dilute urine**.
This is **negative feedback**: the response reverses the change in water content.
ADH is a hormone, so it travels in the **blood** (endocrine control).
The 'anti' in anti-diuretic means it **reduces** the production of dilute urine.
core.h: Controlling the water content of the blood: ADH
core.p: The water content of the blood is monitored by the **brain** and controlled by the hormone **ADH** (anti-diuretic hormone). ADH is released into the blood by the **pituitary gland**. The ADH travels in the blood to the **kidney**, where it affects the **permeability of the kidney tubules** to water. When ADH levels are high, the tubules become **more permeable** and **more water is reabsorbed into the blood**, producing a **small volume of concentrated urine**. When ADH levels are low, **less water is reabsorbed**, producing a **large volume of dilute urine**. This is a **negative feedback** system.

bullets: Stimulus: **too little water** (hot day, exercise, not drinking).
Detector: the **brain** monitors the water content of the blood.
Pituitary releases **more ADH** into the blood.
Kidney tubules **more permeable**, **more water reabsorbed**.
Result: **small volume of concentrated (dark) urine**; blood water content rises.
Without this, cells would lose water by **osmosis**.
core.h: When the blood has too little water
core.p: If you have been sweating or have not drunk enough, the blood becomes more **concentrated** (water content falls). The **brain detects** this change and the **pituitary gland releases more ADH**. ADH makes the **kidney tubules more permeable to water**, so **more water is reabsorbed** into the blood. The water content of the blood rises back toward normal, and a **small volume of concentrated urine** is produced. Without this response the person would become dehydrated and cells would lose water by osmosis.

bullets: Stimulus: **too much water** in the blood (large drink).
Pituitary releases **less ADH**.
Kidney tubules become **less permeable** to water, so **less water is reabsorbed**.
Result: **large volume of dilute (pale) urine**.
Blood water content **falls** to normal.
Both directions together = **negative feedback** control of water balance.
core.h: When the blood has too much water
core.p: If you drink a lot of water, the blood becomes more **dilute** (water content rises). The **brain detects** this and the **pituitary gland releases less ADH**. With less ADH the **kidney tubules become less permeable to water**, so **less water is reabsorbed**. More water therefore stays in the tubule and leaves in a **large volume of dilute urine**. The water content of the blood falls back to normal. This is the second half of the negative feedback loop.

bullets: Kidney failure → **urea and ions build up**, water content cannot be controlled.
**Dialysis** uses a machine with **partially permeable membranes** and dialysis fluid.
The dialysis fluid contains the **same glucose and ion concentration as normal blood**, so useful substances are **not lost** (no net diffusion).
**Urea** is absent from the fluid so it **diffuses out** of the blood.
The fluid is **replaced** (flows past) to keep a **concentration gradient** for diffusion.
Dialysis is needed **regularly** and takes **several hours**; it does not cure kidney failure.
Patients must also control **diet and fluid intake**.
core.p: If the kidneys fail they can no longer remove urea or control water and ion levels, so waste builds up and the person becomes seriously ill. Two treatments are used: **dialysis** and a **kidney transplant**. In **dialysis**, the patient's blood flows between **partially permeable membranes**, surrounded by **dialysis fluid**. The fluid has the **same concentration of useful substances (glucose and ions) as normal blood**, so these are not lost from the blood, whereas **urea, excess ions and water** diffuse into the fluid and are removed. The patient must repeat dialysis **regularly**, typically several times a week for a few hours, usually in hospital or at home.

bullets: The transplant kidney does the **filtering** for the patient.
Needs a **tissue-type match** and a **donor** (living or dead); there is a **shortage** of donors.
The immune system may **reject** the kidney (foreign **antigens**).
**Immunosuppressant drugs** reduce rejection but increase the risk of **infection**.
Involves **major surgery** with risks.
A successful transplant frees the patient from **dialysis**.
A transplanted kidney does not last forever and may need replacing.
core.p: A **kidney transplant** replaces the failed kidney with a healthy **donor kidney**, which then does the work of filtering the blood. It is a **long-term** treatment that frees the patient from regular dialysis, but it has problems. The donor organ must be a good **tissue match** and a suitable donor must be found, and there is a shortage of donors. The body's **immune system** may **reject** the new kidney because it contains **foreign antigens**, so the patient must take **immunosuppressant drugs** for life, which increase the risk of infection. One healthy kidney is enough, so living donors are possible.

bullets: Dialysis: available immediately, **no rejection**, but **frequent, long sessions** and a restricted lifestyle.
Transplant: **no regular sessions**, more normal life, but **donor shortage**, **rejection** risk and **drug** side effects.
Dialysis is often used **while waiting for** a transplant.
Costs: dialysis costs continue; a transplant is often cheaper long term (but surgery and drugs cost).
Quality of life usually **improves with a transplant**.
Use data (waiting times, success rates) to evaluate when given.
core.p: Exam questions may ask you to compare or evaluate the two treatments. **Dialysis** is available straight away and avoids major surgery or rejection, but it is a **life-long, time-consuming** treatment that must be repeated, with restrictions on diet and travel. A **transplant** gives a **more normal life** once it works and is usually **cheaper in the long run**, but needs a **donor**, **surgery** and **immunosuppressant drugs**. The best answers weigh up both sides and give a reasoned conclusion that depends on the patient and the availability of donors.

bullets: Osmosis: water moves from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
Active transport: needs energy, moves substances against the concentration gradient.
Hormones: ADH from the pituitary gland, a negative feedback example like blood glucose and temperature.
Diabetes: when blood glucose is very high some appears in urine.
Immunity: transplant rejection is an immune response to foreign antigens.
Ethics: organ donation, shortages and consent.
Diffusion: dialysis relies on diffusion down concentration gradients.
core.p: Kidney function links to **osmosis and diffusion** (water and urea movement), **active transport** (glucose reabsorption), **hormones and negative feedback** (ADH), **diabetes** (glucose in urine), **enzymes and digestion** (protein broken to amino acids) and **ethics of transplants**. It also links to the immune system through **antigens and rejection**, and to **respiration** (energy for active transport).

exam: 1 mark: state facts, e.g. 'Name the hormone that controls water' → ADH; 'where is urea made' → liver.
2 marks: describe a stage, e.g. 'filtration: small molecules forced out of blood, large ones stay'.
3 marks: explain with a reason: 'less ADH so less water reabsorbed so large volume of dilute urine'.
4 marks (compare dialysis and transplant): two points about each, using 'whereas' and the words rejection, donor, immunosuppressant, regular sessions.

6 marks (extended): describe full sequence for a hot day: sweat, blood more concentrated, brain detects, pituitary releases more ADH, more permeable, more water reabsorbed, small volume of concentrated urine, negative feedback.
Use exact phrases: 'all of the glucose', 'some of the ions', 'as much water as the body needs'.
For ADH say 'permeability of the kidney tubules', not 'ADH tells the kidney'.
For dialysis say 'same concentration of glucose and ions as normal blood so no net movement'.
Calculation questions: show the subtraction for urine volume or the percentage change formula with units (dm3).
Data questions: describe the pattern, quote numbers, then link to ADH or sweat.
'Evaluate' questions: give advantages and disadvantages for both options and a conclusion.
Never write 'sugar' or 'blood is cleaned'; use glucose, filtered and reabsorbed.

mistakes.r: Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids and removed by the kidneys.
mistakes.w: Urea is made in the kidneys.

mistakes.r: The liver deaminates amino acids to form ammonia, then urea.
mistakes.w: The kidney makes urea from amino acids.

mistakes.r: Filtration removes small molecules (including glucose and water) by size; useful substances are then reabsorbed.
mistakes.w: The kidney filters out only waste.

mistakes.r: All glucose is reabsorbed, so none is normally in urine; glucose in urine may indicate diabetes.
ADH is released by the pituitary gland and acts on the kidney.
mistakes.w: ADH is made by the kidney.

mistakes.r: More ADH makes the tubules more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and less, more concentrated urine is produced.
mistakes.w: More ADH makes the kidney produce more urine.

mistakes.r: Dialysis fluid has the same glucose and ion concentration as normal blood so they are not lost.
Rejection is because the immune system recognises foreign antigens on the donor kidney.
mistakes.w: A transplant is rejected because the kidney is the wrong size.

mistakes.r: They suppress the immune system to reduce rejection, which increases risk of infection.
mistakes.w: Immunosuppressants make the new kidney work better.

mistakes.r: Excretion is removal of metabolic waste (urea, CO2); egestion is removal of undigested food.
mistakes.w: Excretion and egestion are the same.

summary: The spec (triple only) asks you to explain how the body removes urea and controls water and ion balance: urea made by deamination in the liver, kidneys filtering the blood and selectively reabsorbing, ADH controlling water reabsorption by negative feedback, and the treatments for kidney failure (dialysis and transplant). It matters because it combines several topics and is often tested as a 6 mark explanation.

terms.d: Removal of waste products of metabolism from the body.
Waste product made in the liver from the breakdown of excess amino acids; excreted in urine.
Removal of the amino group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia.
A toxic substance formed in deamination, converted to urea.
Liquid containing urea, excess ions and excess water, made by the kidneys.
The stage in which small molecules are forced out of the blood into the kidney tubule.
Taking back useful substances (all glucose, some ions, as much water as needed) into the blood.
Anti-diuretic hormone, released by the pituitary gland, which makes kidney tubules more permeable to water.
Endocrine gland that releases ADH in response to the water content of the blood.
A response that reverses a change and returns a condition to its normal level.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
Treatment in which blood is passed over partially permeable membranes in contact with dialysis fluid to remove waste.
Fluid with the same concentration of useful substances as normal blood, but no urea.
Replacing a failed organ with a healthy donor organ.
The immune system attacking a donated organ because it has foreign antigens.
Drug that reduces the activity of the immune system to prevent rejection.
Blood vessels that carry blood to and from the kidney.
Organ that stores urine before it is released.

worked.ans: Model answer: Sweating lowers the blood water content. The brain detects this and the pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood. ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood. A small volume of concentrated urine is produced and the water content returns to normal by negative feedback.
worked.q: Explain how the body responds when a person has sweated heavily on a hot day and has not drunk anything. (6 marks)
steps: Sweating reduces the water content of the blood, so it becomes more concentrated.
The brain detects the change in water content.
The pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood.
ADH travels to the kidney and makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water.
More water is reabsorbed into the blood, so the water content rises.
A small volume of concentrated urine is produced; this is negative feedback.

worked.ans: (a) 1.5 dm3. (b) 0.5 dm3 on the hot day; a decrease of 66.7% (about 67%), because more ADH means more water reabsorbed.
worked.q: A person takes in 2.5 dm3 of water per day: 1.5 from drink, 0.8 from food and 0.2 from respiration. They lose 0.4 dm3 in breath, 0.5 dm3 in sweat and 0.1 dm3 in faeces. (a) Calculate the volume of urine. (2) (b) On a hot day sweat loss rises to 1.5 dm3 with the same intake. Calculate the percentage decrease in urine volume. (3)
steps: (a) Water out other than urine = 0.4 + 0.5 + 0.1 = 1.0 dm3.
(b) Other losses = 0.4 + 1.5 + 0.1 = 2.0 dm3, so urine = 2.5 − 2.0 = 0.5 dm3.

worked.ans: Model answer: Dialysis has to be repeated several times a week for hours, whereas a transplant removes the need for regular sessions. A transplant needs a matched donor and can be rejected by the immune system, so immunosuppressant drugs are needed, whereas dialysis needs no donor and has no rejection risk.
worked.q: Compare dialysis and a kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: dialysis must be repeated regularly whereas a transplant is a long-term solution.
Mark 2: dialysis needs no donor whereas a transplant needs a tissue-matched donor.
Mark 3: a transplant risks rejection by the immune system whereas dialysis does not.
Mark 4: transplant patients take immunosuppressants (risk of infection); dialysis patients have long sessions and dietary restrictions.
